lesson.title: Pinpointing Elements: Indexing Into a List
lesson.summary: How to reach into a list and pull out one specific element using zero-based positions, including the shortcut of negative indices.
lesson.body:
You already learned to pull a single character out of a string using its position, something like word[0] for the first character. Lists support the exact same mechanism, and for the exact same reason: both strings and lists are ordered sequences in Python, so both let you retrieve an individual element by stating its position, called an index, inside square brackets.

Python indexing is zero-based, meaning the first element of a list sits at index 0, not index 1. This trips up nearly every beginner at least once, so it is worth internalizing early: the position number tells you how many elements come before the one you want, and nothing comes before the first element, so it gets 0. For a list with four elements, the valid positive indices are 0, 1, 2, and 3, since the last element sits at index length minus one, not at index length.

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date"]
print(fruits[0])
print(fruits[3])
print(fruits[-1])
print(fruits[-2])

Trace this exactly. fruits[0] is the first element, "apple", so that line prints apple. fruits[3] is the fourth element, since indices run 0, 1, 2, 3 for a four-item list, landing on "date", so that line prints date. Then Python's negative indexing kicks in: fruits[-1] always refers to the last element regardless of how long the list is, which here is also "date", so that prints date again. fruits[-2] refers to the second-to-last element, "cherry", so the final line prints cherry. Altogether the output is apple, then date, then date, then cherry, each on its own line.

Negative indices exist because counting from the end is often more natural than counting from the beginning. If you want the last item in a list of any length, you never have to compute len(fruits) - 1 yourself; you simply write fruits[-1] and let Python handle it, which is both shorter and less error-prone, especially when the list's length can change while your program runs.

Indexing has a firm boundary that slicing, covered next, does not share: asking for an index that does not exist raises an error instead of silently doing something unexpected. Continuing the example above, fruits[4] would raise IndexError: list index out of range, because the list only has valid indices 0 through 3 (or -1 through -4 from the other end). This is Python being strict on purpose. An out-of-range index almost always signals a bug, an off-by-one mistake in a loop, or an assumption about list length that turned out to be wrong, and Python would rather crash loudly right where the mistake happened than let your program silently limp along with the wrong data.

Indexing works identically no matter what the list contains, including lists of strings, numbers, booleans, or even other lists. If you had a list of lists, you would index into the outer list first, such as grid[0], to get the inner list, and then index again, such as grid[0][1], to reach a specific element inside that inner list. That two-step indexing is exactly how you will navigate grids and tables once you start working with nested lists, and it rests entirely on the single-index rules you just traced above.
